data.title: Middle East Eye: Rubio says no 'breakthrough' in US-Iran talks
data.author: Mera Aladam

Rubio says no 'breakthrough' in US-Iran talks
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio suggested that there has been no progress regarding truce talks with Iran, accusing the country of making "unacceptable" demands.
"I don’t have any progress to report to you," Rubio told reporters at the Homestead Air Reserve Base in Florida. "You have a number of countries that continue to engage them with different ideas, but I wouldn’t say we’re on the verge of a breakthrough."
"The president would always prefer to solve this and every problem diplomatically. Sometimes that’s not possible, unfortunately," he added.
Rubio said if there was a chance for a deal, then Washington would "explore it".
"Right now, it hasn’t been very productive because the Iranian demands are simply not just unacceptable, but in some cases outrageous and ridiculous and really not realistic," he said.
His remarks come ahead of his flight to Paris, where he is set to attend the G7 Foreign Ministers meeting on Monday and Tuesday.

Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has dismissed a new US military initiative to restrict the movement of goods through Iran's land borders and the Caspian Sea as “merely wordplay”, as tensions over shipping routes and Washington's blockade continue.
“The Iron Gate plan is merely wordplay. The Americans cannot achieve their objectives of imposing severe economic pressure to cause economic collapse in Iran through this approach,” IRGC spokesman Hossein Mohebbi told the semi-official Fars news agency on Sunday, according to Reuters.
Mohebbi said Washington had previously predicted that Iran would suffer economic collapse within two weeks, but that this had not happened.
Tehran had prepared for economic pressure and maintained close relations with neighbouring countries, he said.
The response came after US Central Command (Centcom) announced the establishment of Task Force Iron Gate on Saturday.

At least five other people were rescued with injuries by Civil Defence search-and-rescue teams at the makeshift camp in Deir al-Balah, where operations to locate missing people continued.
Mahmoud Basal, spokesperson for the Palestinian Civil Defence in Gaza, said the massive sandy embankment and surrounding mounds of earth collapsed after a low-pressure weather system brought torrential rain and strong winds to the Strip over the weekend.
Two of those killed were identified as Mariam Nabhan and her son, Salah Nabhan. The other three were Reem al-Zain, Habiba al-Zain and Ibrahim al-Zain.
Weekend downpours flooded an estimated 70,000 temporary tents sheltering displaced families across Gaza, leaving thousands of people exposed to the elements.

data.author: Alex MacDonald
data.summary:
Iran defends two-day proposal for peace talks after US rejects conditions
Iran defended a proposal on Monday to restart peace talks in as few as two days as the most reasonable offer on the table, after US Secretary of State Marco Rubio called some of Iran's conditions "outrageous and ridiculous".
"Is it unreasonable that Iran demands that US illegal sanctions and its naval blockade must be lifted before negotiations start and that the war should end on all fronts?" Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei told a weekly press conference in response to Rubio's remarks.
Iran has made the offer to shorten the time to restart talks from an earlier seven-day proposal, which calls for Washington to first meet conditions including halting hostilities, lifting a blockade and waiving sanctions.
Baghaei also said US pressure on Iraq to close most of its borders with Iran should not affect bilateral ties with Baghdad, after Iraq's foreign minister said Washington was pushing for such a move. Baghaei dismissed a US military task force aimed at restricting Iran's land trade as a diversion following President Donald Trump's Republicans' losses in midterm elections.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Eminent Ottoman historian Engin Deniz Akarli dies aged 81
data.author: MEE staff
data.summary:
Eminent Ottoman historian Engin Deniz Akarli dies aged 81
Submitted by
MEE staff
on
Mon, 11/09/2026 - 10:33
Professor emeritus at Brown University, Akarli was known for his contributions to the legal, economic and political history of the Ottoman Empire
Professor Engin Deniz Akarli taught classes on world economic history and Middle Eastern and Ottoman history (X/Bisav)
Off
One of the world’s leading scholars of Ottoman history, Engin Deniz Akarli, died in his home in Istanbul on Sunday, aged 81.
Professor Akarli’s research focused on the legal, political and economic history of the late Ottoman Empire, as well as the Middle East. His scholarship engaged deeply with neglected areas of research in these fields.
One of his most influential works, The Long Peace: Ottoman Lebanon, 1861-1920 (University of California Press, 1993) challenged Eurocentric narratives on state-building and governance that centre western intervention through a close study of the Mount Lebanon Mutassarifiya (governorate) following the civil war of 1860.
He demonstrated that Lebanese self-rule, institutions and local religious reconciliation in this period laid the foundations for secular democracy that was hampered by European intervention.
Born in the northwestern Turkish city of Eskisehir, Professor Akarli completed his primary and secondary education at Eskisehir Maarif College, and graduated from the Department of Business Administration and Economics at the prestigious Robert College (now Bogazici University), in 1968.
He continued his education in the United States, first at Wisconsin University for his Master’s studies, and then at Princeton for his PhD.
His teaching career spanned several universities multiple continents. After completing his doctoral studies, he returned to Turkey as one of the founding professors of the history department at Bogazici University.

In response to 'Zionism is racism' motion, Burnham's party is set to break local cooperation deals with the Greens
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham speaks to the media in St. John’s, Antigua and Barbuda, on 4 November 2026 (Kin Cheung/AFP)
Off
The UK Labour Party has signalled its intention to break local co-operation deals with the Green Party over the latter’s “Zionism is racism” motion, passed at the Greens’ conference last month.
Eleven power-sharing agreements with the Greens look set to be terminated, including in Stafford and Warwick councils, where local Green parties have refused to renounce the motion, as demanded by Labour.
Hundreds of thousands of people could be affected as their local councils lose working majorities, with the Labour leadership’s diktat forcing its council groups to either find alternative coalition partners or govern as minority administrations.
Several local coalition agreements have already been ended, with councils being run without a majority in places such as Derbyshire, Havant, and Lewes. Sheffield's Labour-Green joint administration, which governs over half a million people, is holding on after the two groups reached a last-minute deal on 4 November.
The Labour Party, it appears, has decided that ideological conformity on Israel is more important than the needs of residents.
The arrogance of this move is striking. Labour spent the best part of three years backing Israel to the hilt, both militarily and politically, as it inflicted genocide on Gaza, only latterly expressing reservations after coming under increasing domestic and international pressure. Now it presumes the right to lecture the Greens about standards of morality and political hygiene, as if it has any claim to the moral high ground.
